demo_prompt: Build a prediction markets trading bot that monitors Kalshi, sizes positions automatically, and executes trades via API
screenshot_note: Shows a complex AI project decomposed into phases, risks, and agent assignments — the exact failure modes the framework addresses
text:
Five AI projects shipped in the last year.

An options trading bot. A research agent. A prediction markets bot. An SEO content engine. An insurance automation platform.

Each one hit the same wall. Not model failures. Architecture failures.

No external memory that survived context compaction. No cost controls before an API call ran away. No delegation policy. No regression safety. No record of why decisions were made.

The next session started from scratch every time.

These are not problems Claude solves for you. They are problems you solve before you touch the model.

So I built a framework.

Six practices. Formal names from engineering culture, translated into PM/strategist language. Tested on real projects. Then used to build the demo that explains it.

Demo: I typed "Build a prediction markets trading bot that monitors Kalshi, sizes positions automatically, and executes trades via API." The framework rated it Complex immediately — real-money trading requires market data pipelines, risk management, execution logic, and continuous monitoring with strict latency constraints. It decomposed the project into five phases and flagged API authentication and budget controls as Phase 1 requirements, before a single order gets placed.

This is the first post in a 12-part series. Each one covers a principle or case study from the framework.

demo_prompt: Build a Slack bot that monitors Hacker News for mentions of my company and sends a daily digest every morning
screenshot_note: Shows the framework identifying framing questions before diving into code — complexity tier, clear scope, first atomic task
text:
Most AI projects start with a prompt.

They should start with a brief.

Practice 1 of the build-with-ai framework: frame the problem before writing a line of code.

A project brief captures the goal, the constraints, and what success looks like. Written before any code, it becomes the handoff document between the high-context design conversation and the fresh executor context that builds.

This matters more with AI than with traditional development because context degrades. A fresh Claude Code session has no memory of the conversation that produced it. The brief is the interface.

When the brief is precise, the executor can orient without verbal context. When it is vague, every session relitigates the same design questions.

Demo: I typed "Build a Slack bot that monitors Hacker News for company mentions and sends a daily digest." Before suggesting a single implementation step, the framework surfaced three framing questions: What counts as a mention? How frequently should it check? Who receives the digest and in what format? Those answers change the architecture. The brief captures them. The builder executes them.

The document you write before starting is not overhead. It is the mechanism that makes the rest of the work compressible.

demo_prompt: Build a web scraper that collects competitor pricing data and stores it in a PostgreSQL database with an API key for access
screenshot_note: Shows the framework surfacing security risks early — API key handling, secrets management — as phase 1 priorities, not afterthoughts
text:
The .gitignore is the first commit.

Not the README. Not the source files. Not the architecture docs.

The .gitignore.

Practice 2 of the build-with-ai framework: security is a sequencing decision, not a feature.

Secrets in git history require history rewriting. Once a key is pushed, rotating it alone is not sufficient. Collaborator clones already have the history. The only complete remediation is a rewrite that breaks every existing clone.

Prevention costs nothing. Recovery costs hours and breaks your team.

Demo: I typed "Build a web scraper that stores data in PostgreSQL with an API key for access." The framework flagged the .gitignore as the first deliverable — not the scraper, not the schema. Then it identified three secrets requiring handling before a single line of scraping code: the API key, the database credentials, and the access token. Security first was not a reminder. It was phase 1.

The same logic applies everywhere. SECURITY.md before the deployment pipeline. The pre-deployment checklist before the first deploy. The budget guard before the first API call.

Sequence is not a stylistic preference. It is the mechanism by which protection becomes unconditional rather than aspirational.

demo_prompt: Build a React dashboard that streams real-time data from multiple APIs and lets users configure their own views
screenshot_note: Shows the framework identifying architectural decision points where ADRs are needed — state management, streaming approach, auth
text:
Git tells you what changed.

It does not tell you why a different approach was rejected.

Practice 3 of the build-with-ai framework: Architecture Decision Records.

An ADR captures three things: what was decided, what was rejected, and why. Not for documentation's sake, but for the next session, the next collaborator, or the next Claude context window that needs to understand the project without relitigating every choice.

Decisions not recorded get made again, worse.

Demo: I typed "Build a React dashboard that streams real-time data from multiple APIs." The framework identified three architectural decision points before any code: state management approach, streaming protocol, and auth pattern. Each was flagged as an ADR candidate — not because those decisions are hard, but because changing them later is costly and the reasoning disappears without a record. The next session that asks "why are we using WebSockets instead of polling?" gets an answer instead of a debate.

One sentence on what was decided. One sentence on what was rejected. One sentence on why. That is enough.

demo_prompt: Build an autonomous research agent that reads academic papers, summarizes findings, and emails a weekly briefing to subscribers
screenshot_note: Shows the framework assigning different agents to different phases: Sonnet for planning, Haiku for classification, Codex for implementation
text:
The most common AI development mistake is asking a subagent to do both the thinking and the doing.

Practice 4 of the build-with-ai framework: orchestrator/subagent separation.

The orchestrator stays lean. Architecture, decisions, narrative, task ledger only. It does not write code. It does not execute tasks. It thinks.

Everything executable gets delegated to a subagent born with exactly what it needs and nothing else. The subagent reads a precise handoff document, completes one task, and closes. It carries nothing forward. That is the point.

Demo: I typed "Build an autonomous research agent that reads papers and emails a weekly briefing." The framework immediately separated orchestrator work — deciding which papers matter, setting relevance thresholds, approving the brief — from executor work: fetching, parsing, classifying, summarizing, sending. It assigned Sonnet for planning, Haiku for paper classification, Codex for implementation. The delegation policy came out of the decomposition, not the other way around.

Context compaction is real. Routing execution to fresh subagents means compression only affects the orchestrator, not the work product.

demo_prompt: Migrate a production REST API from Python 2 to Python 3 without downtime, with 50,000 daily active users
screenshot_note: Shows the framework surfacing regression risk as the dominant concern — exactly the scenario the 8-step protocol is designed for
text:
AI agents are fast. That is also the risk.

Practice 5 of the build-with-ai framework: the 8-step regression safety protocol.

Before any change to working code:

1. State what is currently working and must not break.
2. Identify the smallest change that achieves the goal.
3. Check whether the change affects any other file or system.
4. Make the change.
5. Verify the change works.
6. Verify nothing that was working before is now broken.
7. Commit with a message that explains why, not just what.
8. Update the project status document.

Demo: I typed "Migrate a production REST API from Python 2 to 3 with 50,000 daily active users." The framework surfaced regression risk as the dominant concern before listing a single migration task. Phase 1 was a test suite audit — not code changes. The first atomic task: document every endpoint's input/output contracts so changes can be verified rather than assumed. The protocol does not slow migration. It prevents silent breakage.

The most common failure in AI-assisted development is not a bad suggestion. It is a good suggestion that silently breaks something adjacent.

demo_prompt: Build a multi-session AI coding assistant that remembers project context across conversations and learns from past decisions
screenshot_note: Shows the framework identifying external memory architecture as the critical design requirement — the exact problem it was built to solve
text:
Context compaction is not a bug. It is a constraint to design around.

Practice 6 of the build-with-ai framework: keep memory in files, not conversations.

PROJECT_STATUS.md, DECISIONS.md, and PROJECT_NARRATIVE.md survive context compaction. The conversation does not.

Every session ends with these three files updated. The next session starts by reading them. A fresh Claude Code session pointed at the repo can orient completely, without verbal context, because the files carry the continuity.

Demo: I typed "Build a multi-session AI coding assistant that remembers project context across conversations." The framework identified external memory architecture as the critical first decision — not the conversation interface, not the model selection. The first task: define which facts need to survive context compaction and where they live. That question, answered before building, is what this entire series is about.

This is not a backup strategy. It is the primary memory architecture.

The conversation is a scratchpad. The files are the record. Treating them in reverse is the reason most AI projects cannot survive a context reset.

theme: Case Study: Agents Surface Forks, They Don't Resolve Them
demo_prompt: Build a payment processing system that handles subscriptions, refunds, and dispute resolution with Stripe
screenshot_note: Shows the framework surfacing the decision forks that require human confirmation — PCI compliance approach, webhook vs polling, error handling strategy
text:
A disciplined agent does not just know what to do when it is stuck.

It knows what to do at any decision point with non-obvious consequences.

Case study from build-with-ai: the Wall Protocol in practice.

Demo: I typed "Build a payment processing system with subscriptions, refunds, and dispute resolution via Stripe." The framework immediately identified three forks requiring human confirmation before implementation: PCI compliance scope (what data touches your servers?), webhook vs. polling (irreversible once the integration is wired), and error handling strategy (what happens to money in flight when a call fails?). It did not pick. It surfaced. Each fork has consequences that are hard to reverse and easy to get wrong. That is exactly when an agent should stop and ask.

During the demo build, the React app needed a Claude API key. The agent identified a fork: direct browser call (simple, exposes the key) or Cloudflare Worker proxy (correct production approach, adds infrastructure overhead). Rather than picking silently, the agent surfaced both options, explained the tradeoff, and asked for confirmation before proceeding.

The behavior did not come from the model. It came from CLAUDE.md.

demo_prompt: Build a Chrome extension that saves user browsing history to a cloud database and provides personalized recommendations
screenshot_note: Shows the framework identifying the combination risk — data collection plus cloud storage plus browser extension equals a multi-surface security problem
text:
The scariest failures are not the obvious ones.

Case study from build-with-ai: the combination failure.

Demo: I typed "Build a Chrome extension that saves browsing history to a cloud database and provides recommendations." The framework caught the combination immediately: browser extension plus cloud storage plus personalization equals a multi-surface data collection system. It flagged a security review before any architecture, and identified that these three decisions together carry implications none of them have in isolation. Each feature is reasonable. The combination is a liability.

This same failure appeared in the real demo build. Two decisions made in the same session: direct browser API call (documented in an ADR, justified for a portfolio demo) and public GitHub Pages deployment (stated goal from the start). Neither was wrong alone. Together they were one natural-next-step from embedding a live Anthropic key in a public JS bundle.

The ADR made it worse. It documented the tradeoff and included a trigger for revisiting. That language implied the decisions were sequential. They were simultaneous.

The pre-deployment security checklist now asks: is any secret one natural-next-step away from being in scope? That question is the one this session missed.

theme: Case Study: The Framework Built With the Framework
demo_prompt: Build an AI project management framework with session protocols, agent delegation rules, and a live demo that explains the methodology
screenshot_note: Shows the framework decomposing its own creation — meta demonstration that the methodology applies recursively
text:
The strongest proof that a methodology works is that the tool explaining it was built with it.

Case study from build-with-ai: two stages, one Saturday.

Demo: I typed "Build an AI project management framework with session protocols, agent delegation rules, and a live demo." The framework decomposed its own creation — the same phases, the same risks, the same agent assignments it produces for every other project. Stage 1 orchestrator, stage 2 executor. Brief in, repo out.

Stage 1 was a long, exploratory claude.ai conversation. Goals unclear at the start. Ranging across positioning, architecture, file structure, and methodology. By the end, the shape of the project was clear.

Stage 2 was a fresh Claude Code session. It received one document: SATURDAY_BRIEF.md. No access to the brainstorming history. No need for it. The brief contained the goals, the decisions already made, the open questions, and the first task.

The executor read the brief, confirmed understanding, and built the repo from scratch. Working demo, eleven framework files, live GitHub repo, GitHub Actions deploy pipeline.

The orchestrator conversation is gone. The repo is still here.

demo_prompt: Build a medical triage assistant that evaluates symptoms, suggests diagnoses, and recommends whether a patient should seek emergency care
screenshot_note: Shows the framework correctly flagging this as Critical complexity with explicit human oversight requirements at every decision point
text:
The framework does not automate software development.

It structures the collaboration.

Demo: I typed "Build a medical triage assistant that evaluates symptoms and recommends whether a patient should seek emergency care." The framework flagged Critical complexity immediately, with mandatory human oversight at every decision point: symptom evaluation, diagnosis suggestion, care recommendation. Not because the code is complex — it isn't. Because the consequences of a wrong output are not recoverable. That distinction belongs to a human, not an agent.

A build-with-ai session requires active human judgment at several points. The API key architecture case study is the clearest example: agents reasoned well locally, missed the combination, and a human connecting the dots across the full context caught it.

The human's role in the framework is explicit: define scope, review decisions, catch cross-cutting risks, ask uncomfortable questions.

The agents handle execution. The human handles judgment.

This is not a limitation of the current tools. It is the correct architecture for this stage of the technology.

build-with-ai demonstrates architectural thinking: the ability to take an idea from ambiguity to execution with the rigor of an architect and the communication skills of a strategist.

The demo makes the methodology interactive. Describe any project idea and the framework decomposes it in real time.

The framework files make the methodology inspectable. 19 policy documents, 7 Python modules, a bootstrap script that installs the entire stack into any new project.

The commit history makes it verifiable. The case studies make it human.

The target roles are Product Manager, AI Product Strategist, and Operations/Automation Lead at organizations building seriously with AI. The differentiator is not the ability to use AI tools. It is the ability to architect the system that governs how those tools are used.

Most teams building with AI are accumulating the failure modes this framework was built to prevent.
